title: The seventy, the seven deacons, and how the four Gospels were written
english: Clement relates in the fifth book of the Outlines that among the seventy apostles of the Savior were Barnabas, Sosthenes, Cephas who had the same name as Peter, Matthias who was numbered with the eleven, Eubulus, Pudens, Crescens, in the second book, Barsabbas and Linus, whom Paul mentions when writing to Timothy (2 Timothy 4:21), along with Thaddaeus, Cleopas, and those with him.
These are the names of the deacons chosen for service: first, Stephen the first martyr; second, Philip; third, Prochorus; fourth, Nicanor; fifth, Timon; sixth, Parmenas; seventh, Nicholas.
The chief ones among the seventy are these: Paul, Mark, Luke, Titus, the eunuch of Candace, and John the Baptist.

It is necessary to know how the four gospels were composed. After the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Gospel according to Matthew came after eight years, the Gospel according to Mark after twelve years, the Gospel according to John after thirty years under King Domitian, and the Gospel according to Luke after fifteen years.

The Gospel according to Matthew was written by him in the Hebrew language in Jerusalem and was published, and it was interpreted by John. The Gospel according to Mark was dictated by Peter in Rome. The Gospel according to Luke was dictated by Paul in Rome. The Gospel according to John was dictated by John himself under Commodus in the times of Trajan, and written on the island of Patmos.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Appendices ad indices apostolorum discipulorumque u01-rem-early
orientation: Epiphanius is listing the seventy apostles and the seven deacons, then recording the dates and circumstances of the four Gospels' composition.

title: Luke's Gospel and its calf-symbol
english: The Gospel according to Luke, however, belongs to Luke, a disciple of the apostle Paul. The same apostle remembers him and writes in a certain letter, “Luke, the beloved physician, greets you” (Colossians 4:14). This same evangelist also composed the acts of the holy apostles. These gospels cannot be more or fewer than this number. For the Gospel according to John recounts his princely, active, and glorious generation from the Father: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; all things came into being through him” (John 1:1, 3). For this reason it bears the symbol of the eagle. The Gospel according to Luke, since it has a priestly character, begins with Zechariah the priest, saying, “In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah” (Luke 1:5), because according to the old tradition of the law the priests brought bulls. For this reason its form is depicted as calf-shaped.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Appendices ad indices apostolorum discipulorumque u01-rem-mid
orientation: The author is explaining the symbolic character of each Gospel, and has just described John's Gospel as the eagle; now he turns to Luke's Gospel and its opening with the priest Zechariah.

title: Matthew and Mark symbols and the return of Mark and Luke
english: Matthew recounts his human birth: “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and again, “Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way” (Matthew 1:18). For this reason his gospel is depicted as formed like a man.

Mark made his beginning from the prophetic Spirit coming down from on high in the heavens. He speaks of the beginning of the gospel (Mark 1:1), as it is written in the prophets: “A voice crying in the wilderness” (Mark 1:3). In this way he displays the prophetic character of the gospel and depicts the image of the lion in the wilderness. Holy Trinity, our God, save us by your grace.

Mark the evangelist was bishop of the Alexandrians, and Luke was the evangelist. These four, from the seventy, were among those who scattered at the preaching in which the Lord said, “Unless anyone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he is not worthy of me” (cf. John 6:51–56, paraphrased). But the one returned to the Lord through Peter, and the other through Paul, and they were deemed worthy to preach the gospel. For his sake they were also martyred, the one burned with fire and the other crucified on an olive tree.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Appendices ad indices apostolorum discipulorumque u01-rem-close
orientation: The author finishes linking Matthew to the man and Mark to the lion, then closes by naming Mark and Luke as men of the seventy who scattered and later returned.
